title: Comparing two ways of positioning a knee replacement in people with knee osteoarthritis and bowed legs
official: Clinical and functional comparison of unrestricted kinematic alignment and mechanical alignment in medial pivot total knee arthroplasty in patients with varus deformity: a randomized clinical trial
summary:
Background and study aims
Knee osteoarthritis damages the joint and can cause pain, stiffness and difficulty walking. When symptoms become severe, knee replacement surgery may be needed. Although this operation helps many patients, some still experience discomfort or feel that their replacement knee does not move naturally.
This study compares two ways of positioning the same knee replacement. Conventional mechanical alignment aims to straighten the leg. Unrestricted kinematic alignment aims to restore the individual knee’s alignment and joint position before arthritis develops. We want to find out whether the second approach makes the replacement knee feel more natural during everyday activities in people with a mildly or moderately bowed leg.

Who can participate?
Men and women aged 50 to 80 years with advanced knee osteoarthritis who need their first total knee replacement at Hospital San Juan de la Cruz de Úbeda, Spain. Their knee must have a mild-to-moderate bow-legged alignment, measuring between 3 and 10 degrees on standing X-rays. The research team will check the other eligibility criteria before offering participation.

What does the study involve?
Participants are randomly allocated to one of two groups. One group will receive conventional mechanical alignment and the other unrestricted kinematic alignment. All participants will receive the same model of knee replacement and the same surgeon will perform all operations.
Participants will be assessed before surgery and at 6, 12 and 24 months afterwards. They will complete questionnaires about pain, daily activities, knee function and how aware they are of their replacement knee. A healthcare professional will measure knee movement. The team will also record complications and any further operations.
The main comparison will be how natural the replacement knee feels during everyday activities 2 years after surgery, measured using a questionnaire.
X-rays will be collected as part of routine care. At 24 months, additional X-rays will only be requested if clinically needed.
Where possible, participants and the professional assessing their knee will remain unaware of the assigned technique. Participants can request this information, and information needed for their medical care will always be provided.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no guarantee of an additional personal benefit from taking part. The findings may help surgeons choose the most suitable approach for future patients.
Both surgical approaches are used in clinical practice. The usual risks of knee replacement surgery remain, including infection, blood clots, stiffness, instability, persistent pain and the possible need for another operation. The protocol does not anticipate substantial additional risks beyond those of routine knee replacement. Participation also involves time spent completing questionnaires and assessments.
Taking part is voluntary. Participants may withdraw at any time without affecting their medical care.

Where is the study run from?
Hospital San Juan de la Cruz de Úbeda (Spain)

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to April 2030

Who is funding the study?
Investigator initiated and funded. The study will use the staff, implants, equipment and clinical services routinely available at Hospital San Juan de la Cruz de Úbeda.

Who is the main contact?
Dr Salvador Aznar Zafra, salvador.aznar.sspa@juntadeandalucia.es
conditions: Advanced primary knee osteoarthritis with mild to moderate constitutional varus deformity, requiring primary total knee arthroplasty

interventions.name: Participants will be randomly allocated in a 1:1 ratio to two parallel groups. The allocation sequence will be generated using Randomizer.at with variable permuted blocks of four and six. Allocation will be concealed using sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes opened after definitive enrol

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age between 50 and 80 years, inclusive
2. Advanced primary knee osteoarthritis with an indication for primary total knee arthroplasty
3. Mild to moderate constitutional varus deformity, defined as mechanical varus between 3° and 10°, inclusive, measured using the hip–knee–ankle (HKA) angle on a standing full-length lower-limb radiograph
4. Ability to understand and complete the study questionnaires
5. Willingness to participate and provision of written informed consent
Exclusion criteria:
1. Valgus knee deformity or mechanical varus greater than 10°
2. Relevant previous surgery on the knee to be operated on
3. Significant ligament instability
4. Inflammatory arthropathy
5. Revision knee arthroplasty
6. Body mass index (BMI) greater than 35 kg/m²
7. Inability to attend follow-up visits or complete the study questionnaires
8. Severe medial bone defects requiring reconstruction, augments or revision implants
